effectiveRainFraction.source: K-State, Efficient Crop Water Use in Kansas (MF3066, August 2012), Chapter 3, Table 9 and the text beside it: a simulated water budget for dryland corn on a northwest Kansas silt loam, with 19.24 inches of average annual precipitation, 14.40 inches of evapotranspiration, 3.90 inches of interception, 0.94 inch of runoff and no percolation. https://bookstore.ksre.ksu.edu/pubs/MF3066.pdf
effectiveRainFraction.assumption: No source opened gives one share of rain that a dryland crop can use in Kansas. In this simulated budget 14.40 of 19.24 inches, about 75 percent, became evapotranspiration. That figure includes water evaporated from the soil, so reading it as the share a crop can use is the tool's own. The tool counts 75 percent of the rain in a crop's season as usable, everywhere in Kansas.

fallowEfficiency.source: Nielsen and Vigil (2010), Precipitation Storage Efficiency during Fallow in Wheat-Fallow Systems, Agronomy Journal 102(2):537-543, USDA-ARS, Akron, Colorado: over the 14-month fallow of a wheat-fallow system, precipitation storage efficiency averaged 20 percent with conventional tillage (range 8 to 34) and 35 percent with no-till (range 20 to 51). https://www.ars.usda.gov/ARSUserFiles/30100500/Publications%202010-2019/544%20Nielsen%20Vigil%20-%20Precipitation%20storage%20efficiency%20during%20fallow%20in%20wheat-fallow%20systems.PDF
fallowEfficiency.assumption: The study measured one kind of bare period: the 14-month fallow between wheat crops. The tool applies its conventional-tillage average, 20 percent, to every bare period in every rotation, which is the tool's simplification. Measured values differ by tillage and rotation: no-till averaged 35 percent in the same study, and K-State measured 15 to 28 percent before wheat at Tribune, Kansas, in 2008 to 2019 (Schlegel, Haag and Burnett, 2020, https://journals.newprairiepress.org/kaesrr/article/11125/galley/11018/download/).
